speaker: Alice Jordan-Baird
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
I rise today to raise the voices of community concerns in the outer west. In my community in Melbourne's western suburbs, there's been a proposal for the largest data centre ever publicly proposed in Australia. At 350 hectares, the Plumpton data centre project will cover the equivalent of 175 MCG playing fields. People in our community are rightly asking questions about what a development of this scale could mean for our growing suburbs. I want to take this opportunity in this parliamentary chamber to say that I hear the concerns about the potential impact on local energy and water resources, the increased traffic movements and noise, and the cumulative pressure placed on infrastructure that is already struggling to keep pace.

These are the right questions to be asking. They reflect a community who want to understand how a major industrial development would affect their quality of life, local environment and future of our region. As AI demand and reliance on cloud computing grows, data centre investment in Australia is necessary. But—in our community, near homes and close to schools—data centre development must happen in ways that deliver positive outcomes for the community.

The Albanese Labor government has set out clear expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure built here to ensure that investments provide tangible benefits both locally and across Australia. Operators must prioritise Australia's national interests, not only by strengthening our security and resilience but also by delivering benefits to local communities. They are also expected to support the energy transition with new renewable energy and to not put upward pressure on energy prices, to manage water responsibly, to create well-paid jobs and local skills, and to back startups, research, innovations and supply chains.

I will not support data centre developments that fail to meet these expectations. Our community deserves clear answers, genuine consultation and transparent planning processes. The west cannot simply become the destination for infrastructure that places additional strain on resources while delivering little in return. I will continue to listen to residents, seek answers on their behalf and advocate strongly for the long-term visibility, sustainability and wellbeing of our growing community.

speaker: Lord Houghton of Richmond
heading: Military Conflicts: International Law - Question
text: My Lords, we are in the process of vetting the House on the future of military capability enabled by artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems, but human agency will remain the paramount factor in ensuring that these systems conform to the legal and moral constraints of warfare. Those constraints, both international humanitarian law and the laws of armed conflict, are themselves diverging. The pressures and burdens on individuals in the Armed Forces—the agents of the state—will become ever greater and so, therefore, will the need to protect them. Do the Government fully recognise this, and what are they doing about it?

speaker: Anneliese Dodds
subheading: Societal Impact of AI: Government Policy
text:
I absolutely agree. That phenomenon of so-called cognitive offloading and the lack of scaffolding in skills is a genuine concern. Equally, we see how rapidly and accurately AI can assess tumour scans, for example, working with human beings to deliver the highest possible quality of healthcare. I agree with my hon. Friend the Member for Camborne and Redruth (Perran Moon) about the potential there. We need to have a sensible approach to this issue.

I also want to mention some additional harms. We are now seeing ubiquitous slop on the internet, AI-enabled fraud and cyber-attacks, and the impact of AI summaries on local media use as well, so I want to see the CMA using its powers for competition-focused action on strategic market status services. I want the Government to adopt a maximalist approach to the “Watch this Space” White Paper, and I want us to stop treating bots as separate, because AI is increasingly going to be integral to our interface with the internet, as well as to so much else, so we need to adopt a safety-by-design approach to online regulation, and that needs to recognise the increasing ubiquity of AI.

speaker: Helen Beatrice Polley
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
I rise as Chair of the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Law Enforcement to speak to the committee's report for the inquiry into the capabilities of law enforcement to respond to money laundering and financial crime. Money laundering is not a victimless crime. It is the engine that powers organised crime, recycling those profits into further criminal activities. Money laundering corrodes our financial institutions, undermines our financial system and ultimately harms every Australian. The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission conservatively estimates that approximately $38 billion in proceeds of crime was available for laundering in Australia in 2023-24 alone. That figure does not capture overseas proceeds brought into Australia for laundering, which are assessed to be significant.

This inquiry was initiated by the 47th Parliament and reaffirmed in the 48th Parliament with a refreshed committee. The inquiry examined the scale of money laundering, Australia's legislative framework, law enforcement's capabilities and challenges, information issues and the role of the private sector. The committee heard from federal agencies, state and territory police forces, the private sector, academics and many other witnesses, and we appreciate their evidence. The breadth and quality of that evidence helped to shape a report the committee is proud to present, as we did two weeks ago.

The evidence before the committee painted a picture of a threat that is growing in scale, sophistication and complexity. Technology is at the heart of the evolution. Criminal networks are also exploiting international trade systems in ways that are difficult to detect and hard to prosecute. The committee was encouraged to hear that our federal agencies are embracing new tools. AUSTRAC is trialling AI to analyse half a million suspicious matter reports it receives each year. The AFP has made AI adoption a key priority under its new commissioner. The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission is building AI literacy across its workforce, and, through partnerships like the Fintel Alliance and the Australian Financial Crimes Exchange, the public and private sectors are beginning to share intelligence in ways that would have been impossible a decade ago.

One of the most consistent themes in the evidence was the problem of information—who has it, who needs it, and what the law currently allows to be shared. Information sharing between agencies and the private sector is improving but also remains restrained.

During the inquiry period, the government reduced information gaps by expanding Australia's anti-money-laundering and counterterrorism financing regime to capture lawyers, accountants, real estate agents and others. This reform addresses a significant vulnerability, making sure that professional services are aware that they need to report and should be reporting suspicious activities.

The beneficial ownership register, which would make it far harder for criminals to hide behind complex corporate structures and shell companies, remains, unfortunately, years away. The committee understands these sequences but urges that this work be progressed as quickly as possible.

The committee received evidence that recruiting, training and retaining personnel with the specific financial, technological and analytical skills required to combat modern money laundering is one of the most pressing challenges facing the law enforcement agencies. This is not simply a human resource problem; it is a national security problem. Getting the workforce settings right is fundamental.

In total, the committee makes 10 recommendations, and they are designed to close the gaps in the legislative framework. I also want to acknowledge not only the witnesses who gave evidence but also the work that is done by Australia's law enforcement and intelligence officers and regulatory agencies, who are working to address these issues every single day. As I said from the outset, money laundering impacts every Australian. We need to do more. We must do more. I put on record my thanks to the secretariat for the work they did and to my colleagues on the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Law Enforcement for their work and their dedication to bringing this report to the parliament.

speaker: Ian Sollom
heading: Economic Growth
text: The Minister cites our world-class universities and an ambition to double the number of UK unicorns that run frontier technologies such as quantum and AI, but does she recognise that those breakthroughs often come from the curiosity-driven frontier physics research in our universities, and that that research base now faces a £700 million funding gap?

speaker: Mehreen Faruqi
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Strengthening Enforcement for the Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
The Online Safety Amendment (Strengthening Enforcement for the Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2026 is supposed to be about keeping children safe online, but it barely scratches the surface of the much uglier truth. Something deeply disturbing is happening to our young people. A teenage boy opens TikTok or YouTube looking for gym videos or gaming clips. Before long, the algorithm starts pushing him somewhere much darker. They are being told women are liars, feminism is the enemy, and girls owe you sex. When a Herald journalist posed online as a 17-year-old boy, it took just 13 minutes for TikTok to serve up manosphere content—13 minutes for the algorithm to start pulling a child down a rabbit hole of vile misogyny. This stuff doesn't just stay on a screen. Teachers are seeing boys parrot Andrew Tate in classrooms. Researchers are finding terrifying attitudes towards women, consent and sexual violence amongst teenage boys and young men.

These algorithms are teaching boys how to see girls, and girls are living with the consequences. They are sexually harassed, abused, choked, assaulted, raped and killed, and those same girls opened their own phones to be bombarded with content telling them they are too fat or too ugly as thinspo and the latest skinny-tok trend take over their feeds. They see other women being mocked and trolled. They are fed content about eating disorders, self-harm and suicide. Seventy per cent of Australian children aged 10 to 15 have encountered harmful content online. This isn't some harmless teenage entertainment. We have handed some of the most powerful corporations on earth direct access to our children's minds, and they are poisoning them for profit.

These platforms have become some of the most powerful radicalisation machines humanity has ever created. Racism, misogyny, Islamophobia, conspiracy theories, far-right propaganda—the algorithm doesn't care how dangerous something is. It cares whether you keep watching. Watch one angry video, and it gives you another. Show an interest in one conspiracy, and it offers you something more extreme. Linger on some racist garbage, and suddenly your feed is overflowing with it. Now AI slop, deepfakes and industrial scale misinformation are pouring into that toxic soup, which is fuelled by the far right and their wealthy backers. I should know. I am a perpetual target.

Tech oligarchs and their loyal politicians have helped build an information system where hate and lies reach millions in an instant, giving extremists an algorithm that helps them recruit. This is radicalisation at an industrial scale. Instead of fighting the far right and instead of fighting racism and misogyny, some of the richest corporations on earth deliver them straight into our kids' pockets.

Behind these big tech and social media machines are some of the richest and most powerful men who have ever lived—men like Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk. Zuckerberg has amassed billions upon billions building deliberately addictive platforms that harm children. Elon Musk bought one of the world's biggest social media platforms, gutted its safety features and turned himself into a political powerbroker. These are not quirky tech geniuses playing with apps. These are evil men controlling what billions of people see, believe and fear. Their corporations profit from our anger and our fear.

The Greens support stronger enforcement against corporations that break the law, but taking on this crisis means taking on some of the richest and most powerful companies and billionaires on earth. Let's be real. Labor hasn't got a great track record of taking on corporations and billionaires, but the community advocates and Greens have pushed them all the way to take the steps that they have announced today. The details of the proposed duty of care model will be a test of whether Labor backs the people or the corporations in the struggle for our attention and wellbeing. To start, we can't have a situation where harmful algorithms remain the highly addictive default. Then we have to make sure penalties for social media oligarchs are more than a slap on the wrist or just another court settlement for them. We won't change their behaviour until we threaten their noxious business model.

We will be looking at the proposal extremely closely, because history teaches us that, when the choice is between corporate profits and real people being harmed, Labor always finds a way to protect profits. Boys can be funnelled into misogyny. Girls can be taught to hate their bodies. Racism and far-right extremism can be pumped into millions of homes. Our democracy can be flooded with lies. God forbid Mark Zuckerberg's bottom line takes a hit!

Enough of that. We need to break the toxic algorithms and hold these corporations legally responsible for the harms that they create. Our children—and everybody else, for that matter—do not exist to generate profits for billionaires. Our democracy is not theirs to dismantle, and our future should not be determined by Mark Zuckerberg or Elon Musk and wherever their next billions come from.

speaker: Nita Green
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Strengthening Enforcement for the Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2026; In Committee
text:
First of all, we are traversing between two pieces of legislation, so I'm going to address the amendment to this bill that is in front of us. Out of respect for senators, I want to give some indication of the government's approach to digital duty of care. But I cannot, for the remaining 10 minutes, do a rule-in, rule-out game around a piece of legislation that has not been introduced to the parliament. What I will say is that the government doesn't support this amendment to this bill, because it does not meet the core objectives of the social media minimum-age law, which is to delay children's access to a social media account and, in turn, prevent children from being sucked down toxic rabbit holes, as being suggested, of harmful content.

The social media minimum age bill and the amendments we seek to make are not about the algorithm being more transparent. This is about protecting vulnerable children from it altogether. Making the algorithm more transparent, though, and giving adults more choice over how algorithms work is an issue where the government is willing to work with the coalition, with the Greens, across the chamber on our digital duty of care bill. Digital duty of care will include an Australian first, the My Feed, My Way initiative, which gives Australians control over their social media algorithms. This will ensure that children are protected from harmful content and features, including chatbots, gaming platforms, apps and messaging platforms. And users can choose to opt in to have their default feed include personalised content recommended by the algorithm.

What we will seek to do, as we consult on this bill in the consultation process on the draft legislation, is help to ensure that the law is developed and that Australians can benefit from better protections from seriously harmful illegal content across digital services and social media. Users will be afforded more choice. So we will seek, through the consultation process, to understand those issues around transparency. We will work with other senators. We will work with stakeholders. We will work with researchers. I understand that there's a researcher named Rys Farthing who has developed quite a lot of research around this issue of transparency.

But what I'd say to you, through you, Chair, is that the bill before us is not the right place for this amendment. The bill in front of us is about increasing the powers to an obligation on big tech companies to ensure that under-16s cannot access their services at all. There is no access to the algorithm at all under the social media ban. What we will seek to do under digital duty of care, particularly through the My Feed, My Way initiative, is work with stakeholders, with people around the chamber, on what that transparency and accountability should look like, but ultimately ensuring that social media platforms will be required to send a notification to new and existing users, offering them a choice over their default feed. That is a very important step forward.

But of course, as I said at the beginning of my contribution, it's not appropriate for me to rule in or out what particular provisions will be in a piece of legislation that has not yet been introduced and that we are still consulting on. But I want to give an indication to senators who have a very deep interest in this area that we will obviously consider any amendments or any proposals put forward through that process.

It is very important that we pass this bill. This bill relates to stronger powers for the eSafety Commissioner to implement the social media age restrictions, ensuring that children don't have access to social media accounts and are prevented from being impacted in any way by algorithms. We've recognised the harm that they cause. We've recognised that children need more time to form digital literacy, and that's why we've brought this bill forward. But, of course, the digital duty of care bill looks at the broader scope of that content for children and for adults and at how we can hold those big tech companies to account to ensure that their platforms are safe for Australians to use. That is how we'll approach this. That's why we're not supporting this amendment.

In saying that, I appreciate that senators will have times when they want things done expediently and times where they want full scrutiny. I don't think it's fair to say that this particular type of amendment would have been fully scrutinised. At this point, we would want to consider a number of issues, particularly in relation to significant challenges around international intellectual property law. These are all the things that we will take into account, but we will make sure that our new laws deliver for Australians, that we consult on them over the next few weeks and that we have an opportunity for this parliament to debate those laws.

This legislation before us, though, is all about making sure that the laws passed by this parliament require social media companies to do the right thing and to take the right steps, and there will be arguments across this chamber criticising the government's approach. Those are political points that are allowed to be made, but, at the end of the day, these big platforms and big tech companies, I believe, do have the ability to prevent under-16s from using their platforms, and what we need to do is give the eSafety Commissioner the powers to enforce those laws.

This amendment in front of us is not about giving the eSafety Commissioner more transparency or more accountability; the bill before us does that. It provides those information-gathering powers. It provides examination powers. It provides powers that are very similar to the original bill that was championed and introduced by the coalition. We want to make sure that the eSafety Commissioner has all of the tools that she needs to bring big tech companies to account, and that is what the bill before us does.

speaker: Lucy Powell
heading: Education and Skills Reform
text: I hear what the hon. Gentleman is saying. I know my own hairdresser and her team really well—they do a great job on my hair. [Interruption.] Thank you. Indeed, the hairdressers here in the Commons do a great job for me and for the Deputy Speakers. Hairdressing is a job that AI is never going to do—AI is not going to be colouring or cutting my hair any time soon. These are good careers for young people, so we need to look at the barriers to entry. An apprenticeship in a hair salon was once a clear pathway into work, but for many reasons those numbers are falling, and that is something we need to look at.

speaker: Gideon Amos
heading: Water Management
text:
My hon. Friend is characteristically right, and I will come on to schedule 3 to the Flood and Water Management Act 2010, which he and I tried on several occasions to have enacted during the passage of the Planning and Infrastructure Bill.

Crucially, decentralised water management delivers the benefits I have listed: homes that are more resilient, bills that are lower, streets that flood less and rivers that have less sewage being discharged into them. Before I was elected as an MP, my campaign was to get the River Tone designated as a bathing water at French Weir. Working with the friends’ group, we succeeded, but unless we take action to reduce sewage volumes in the Tone catchment and around the country, we will not be able to meaningfully reduce sewage discharges into those rivers and beaches.

Crucially, none of this requires an AI data centre to make it happen; what is required is a shift in mindset: managing rain before it becomes a problem rather than using it to make a problem and then trying to manage that problem we have created. We can personally do our bit. My son thinks that the enormous water butt I am trying to make in my back garden is a Heath Robinson creation—well, he would if he knew what Heath Robinson was, but he is far too young. Following all the regulations is challenging, but I am working on it. However, what is really needed is the Government to take action on regulation.

Three key changes are needed from the Government. First, we need to stop designing homes that treat rain as an inconvenience to be sent elsewhere. Rather, it should be sent into people’s homes and harnessed as the asset and essential natural resource that it is and require rainwater harvesting in all new homes. Secondly, the Government needs to bring schedule 3 of the Flood and Water Management Act into law, as pointed out by my hon. Friend the Member for Didcot and Wantage (Olly Glover), so that we start to drain more of our rainwater into the ground where it falls and have a properly regulated system for doing so. Thirdly, the Government need to grant the retro-splitting of household drains so that people can save on their bills and at the same time save our rivers—like our precious Tone—which can be spared the sewage these drains create, add to and augment.

England is about to spend unprecedented sums on water sewerage and infrastructure. We cannot solely rely on carbon-heavy centralised systems. We should finally change our relationship with the rain that falls right on the top of us all. If we want cleaner rivers, secure water supplies, lower emissions and homes fit for a changing climate, the answer is learning to value rain and use it to save us all money where it lands.

speaker: Dai Le
heading: BUSINESS
text:
I second the motion of the member for Calare. I spoke last week about the good and the bad of this new world we're living in of artificial intelligence—its ability to make us work more efficiently and more productively but also its potential harm to humanity.

Let me start with what artificial intelligence gets right. It can reduce paperwork for small businesses, improve services and help people work more productively, if used well. For small-business owners in Fowler, that matters. A task that once took a day may take an hour. Paperwork that kept someone at the kitchen table late at night can be dealt with before they open the shop in the morning. I, too, want the people of Fowler to have every safe AI tool that helps them compete, grow and spend more time with their families. I'm not here to stand in the way of that.

But a tool this powerful needs rules and guardrails. We are already seeing the harm. For a community like Fowler, the risk can be even greater. More than six in 10 people in Fowler speak a language other than English at home. A scam can arrive in someone's first language sounding urgent and convincing while a legitimate warning does not reach them the same way and at the same speed. An increasing example is AI voice cloning imitating loved ones and demanding money. Once that content spreads, it is hard to pull back. And when people cannot tell what is real, trust breaks down—trust in information, trust in institutions and trust in our democracy.

That's why I support this motion and the member for Calare's bill. It is not about banning AI; it is about keeping people in control of a powerful technology. The bill requires providers of certain advanced AI systems to maintain the ability to intervene, stop a system's outputs, suspend access, restrict dangerous uses or shut the system down when necessary. This is not a one-big-red-button action. It is a graduated response—restrict a harmful capability; slow the system down; suspend access; move to a safe backup; shut it down when there is no safe alternative. That is not anti innovation; it is common sense.

For example, many of you who use today's cars would have—my car at least has it—a reversing safety sensor. So, when I'm reversing out of a car park or my driveway for instance, even though I can see an oncoming car, my car senses an oncoming car and automatically stops my car from reversing further. That way, we do not collide, or there's a prediction that we can collide. Sometimes, it's annoying to use, because I think I have my driving under control. But it has been designed to protect me and others from a mistake that I may not see coming. So we accept that safety feature because we understand the cost of getting it wrong. If we expect safety systems in cars on our driveways, surely we should expect meaningful safety systems from the companies developing the most powerful technology of our time.

There's also a physical side to the AI revolution—data centres, as the member for Calare mentioned. AI does not exist only on our screen; it needs enormous infrastructure, using electricity and water and land. Australia has around 165 operational data centres, with at least 225 more proposed or under development, and they are being fast-tracked before any legislation to safeguard them is in place. They are being built as we speak. Much of that growth is in New South Wales and Victoria. At least two data centres have been approved in Fowler, with more proposed. People deserve answers. Who pays for the electricity, the water and the infrastructure? Can the government guarantee that Fowler families will not face higher power bills? This needs to be addressed, and the member for Calare has done so in this bill.

I welcome innovation. But innovation must serve the people, not leave them behind. And this bill is a sensible step towards responsible planning, stronger safeguards and putting ethics back into infrastructure like data centres and AI development. We need to have that in place, and we have to do that—if we're taking the lead in the world with other legislation, such as the banning of social media for under-16s, surely this is more critical. This will have wider impact on our community and our society.

That is how we can make AI work for Australians. Rather than asking Australians to simply adjust to AI, we need to ensure that the Australian public can trust this new technology that's being rolled out so fast in front of us. Thank you.

speaker: David Shoebridge
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise first of all to acknowledge the work of my colleague Senator Faruqi in this space, endorse her comments and particularly note the raft of concerns about this bill that remain unaddressed including the genuine cost-of-living crisis that we know students are facing with ever mounting HECS debt. I haven't spoken to a student who remembers getting a haircut on the HECS debt, but I've spoken to plenty of students who are looking at a lifetime of debt for simply wanting to get an education to contribute to society.

We still don't see a solution for the so-called Job-Ready Graduates scheme that saw these appalling cost hikes for arts degrees. It was a conscious attack from the coalition to dumb down our universities and to attack critical thinking. We're five years—it feels like forever—into a Labor government, and they still haven't addressed that despite repeated offers from the Greens to solve that. Degree costs have continued on their upward path. Student payments remain below the poverty line. These are the core issues in the university sector that despite the name on the box of this bill—it's called the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026. Again, as we know, the doors of opportunity are very narrowly open under Labor, particularly for students who don't have family support, those who are first generation at university, those who are considering career that isn't in the finance sector or a highly paying sector but is essential for our society like teaching, nursing, social work, critical thinking. They're the ones who continue to be under the gun despite five years of a Labor government.

There's one other thing that I think absolutely needs to be addressed with urgency in the university sector, and it's playing out in university campuses in my home state of New South Wales. It's playing out on the campuses of the University of New South Wales, of the University of Sydney, of UTS, of Macquarie University, but I know it's playing out across universities Australia wide. While there's talk of building opportunities—what this bill talks about—what students and academics are facing right now are universities reaching for AI to dumb down degrees, to replace staff and to put at risk the reputations of some of our finest institutions. Last week, the University of New South Wales said it had signed this so-called strategic partnership with OpenAI—a US owned, tech-bro owned vampire company who has no interest in building Australia's education sector, who has no interest in educating Australians and who definitely has no interest in our universities being competitive. Without putting any guardrails in, without talking to the staff and without articulating what the strategic partnership will mean for job security, for the quality of degrees, for teaching, they make this big announcement. This is the statement that UNSW made:

The collaboration, one of the largest AI education deployments in the Asia-Pacific region, aims to help ensure graduates are equipped to use AI critically, ethically and effectively.

Who are they partnering with? OpenAI, the same US tech-bro owned corporation that let its agents escape the sandbox and run wild.

What are the what are the checks and balances being proposed here? Where are the restraints in how our university sector rolls out AI to endanger our research capability? It's not all upside with AI. There's serious risk of deskilling our researchers, rogue AI agents taking that research and heading off heaven knows where. There's complete silence from this government about—not a whisper about one of our premier universities and, at different times, one of our highest ranked university on global ratings uncritically rolling out a foreign multinational AI player right throughout its universities in what it describes as 'the largest AI education deployment in the Asia-Pacific'.

That's not a good news story. That's a flashing-lights warning story. It's not just that. Less than a week after that, the University of Sydney made an announcement as well. The University of Sydney comes out and talks about 'a university-wide investment in AI to ensure every student and staff member has free and equitable access to advanced AI tools'. And then we get this guff:

Tomorrow's leaders will also need to understand AI's ethical, social and environmental impacts, and possess the ability to work with this technology critically and responsibly. We will support you for that future by providing equitable access to advanced AI tools.

Whatever the University of Sydney's Vice President of Operations, Ms Gower, might say about it being a human centred approach to AI, ask the staff—the academics, the people who are going to have to deliver for this. How they see this deal of the University of Sydney with the same bunch of US tech-bro AI vampires is as a threat. Because, at the same time that the university went out and made its announcement that they're going to be incorporating a foreign owned AI into every aspect of the university's operations, the NTEU members, the people who actually have to teach, do the research and undertake the critical thinking at University of Sydney, were out on strike seeking enforceable consultation protections around AI. This is how this is how managerial and out of touch management at our universities is—these vice-chancellors and their cronies that hang around them, paid a million bucks a year and more. I think, in Sydney, they also get a free, posh residence. You get a million bucks in your bank account and a free, posh residence if you're the vice-chancellor in Sydney, and then you use that privilege to roll out AI and take away the jobs of the actual teaching staff.

And we get Labor coming in here with their—what is it named?—Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill. Well, under Labor, the door's been opened to vampire, US owned AI to come and march through our universities and take away jobs, destroy the critical thinking that we're going to need for our students and continue to empower the managerial class to run through our universities.

I want to say, on behalf of my party, the Greens, that we stand in solidarity with the NTEU members who are on strike, asking for genuine, enforceable consultation protections before universities like Sydney or UNSW enter into these multiyear deals. And we want to make sure that they're enforceable rights so that the vice-chancellors on their million bucks a year and their $500,000, $700,000, $800,000 per annum human-development staff-squashing managerial teams don't get to destroy our universities. The only door of opportunity that seems to be opening here is the door of opportunity for US big tech to come in, deskill and put at enormous risk some of our most important institutions.

I would urge the government to go and look at what the community thinks about this and the lack of action on protecting our universities from the rollout of US owned AI, because you have a look at the comments on social media about Sydney university's post and they're not saying: 'Oh, amazing—wonderful opportunity. I'm glad you've invited these robber barons in to come and attack our university.' They're calling it 'despicable garbage'. They're calling it 'fascism-maxxing'. They're naming it for what it is.

There's some marginal good in this bill. The marginal good is great. But there's this massive risk, and it's not academic; it happened last week—the week before this bill got rolled in to literally destroy the integrity, the reputation, the qualities of our universities, because, under Labor, US big tech, US AI companies, are marching through our universities, and the staff are on the front lines fighting it, going into industrial action, saying, 'You can't do this without us.'

What's the answer from Labor? Nothing, because it turns out that the same big tech companies that are talking to the vice-chancellor at Sydney university and schmoozing with the vice-chancellor at UNSW are in there with a ready-access door to the Prime Minister, trying to do a job on creatives and trying to get a red carpet to roll out their AI vision right across this country—to steal our water, our power and our data and, in this case, to have that march through some of our most important institutions.

Unless this government is willing to come and work with the Greens to address the risk of AI through our universities—you can pass as many 'opening the doors of opportunity' bills as you like, but, unless we address the risk of foreign owned AI through the march of our institutions, this won't amount to a hill of beans.

speaker: Vanessa Bleyer
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
Off the far north-west coast of Tasmania is an island, Robbins Island. Its traditional Palawa name is Pilitika. It is rich in Aboriginal cultural heritage and of profound significance to the Palawa Pakana people. It contains landforms of global geological and geomorphological significance. Its complex coastal systems serve as an international index site for studying past climate changes and sea-level histories. It is on the migratory pathway of the critically endangered orange-bellied parrot, which doesn't just instinctively fly over but stops and forages on the island. It is home to the last remaining disease-free population of the endangered Tasmanian devil in the world. Elsewhere in Tasmania, a facial tumour disease is decimating Tasmanian devil populations.

Now, wait for this, and I hope you're all sitting down: last year, in 2025, this Labor government approved a wind farm at Pilitika/Robbins Island. Construction of turbines will destroy sites of Aboriginal cultural heritage, destroy sites of global geological significance and cause the extinction of the orange-bellied parrot as the turbine blades pulverise the last parrots that survive. Construction of a bridge from mainland Tasmania to Pilitika/Robbins Island will introduce diseased Tasmanian devils and decimate the last healthy wild population. Construction of a wharf will deprive us forever of studying sea-level histories at a time of climate crisis, when we need it most. Like every development, there's a right place and a wrong place. This is simply the wrong place for a wind farm.

You'll be pleased to know I'm the bearer of good news. Something has just happened which means that this government should now bring the proposed wind farm at Pilitika/Robbins Island to an end. It was a condition of this government's approval of the Robbins Island wind farm that, within six months of the date of approval, the proponent of the wind farm—backed by a megarich Philippines based company, by the way—must submit an orange-bellied parrot survey plan to this government for approval. The proponent did not. It was a condition of this government's approval that the proponent notify this government within two business days of failing to comply with the condition. The proponent did not. The big foreign corporation behind the proposed wind farm obviously cares not for the laws of this nation, just like it obviously cares not for the irreplaceable natural and cultural wonders of Pilitika-Robbins Island.

On the other hand, we hear this government talking so much about how it upholds the rule of law and that the rule of law is a foundational principle of Australia's democracy. It follows that it must care very much for the laws of this nation. So, no doubt, this government is going to do what the law says that it should because of the breached conditions and immediately revoke the approval of the wind farm at Pilitika-Robbins Island. No doubt, this government is going to do what the law says it should and prosecute the proponent for its serious statutory offence in breaching the conditions. Surely this government is not more concerned about appeasing a big corporation and making decisions for that big corporation instead of for us. I and so many whom I represent in Tasmania eagerly await the news from this Labor government that it will adhere to the rule of law and that this monstrosity of a wind farm—100 turbines, each over 200 metres high, and in absolutely the wrong place—is over.

Speaking of developments that are absolutely in the wrong place, I note a proposed data centre in the Tamar Valley in northern Tasmania that remains controversial. Recently, a local council in Tasmania approved that AI data centre at what was previously the site for Gunns proposed pulp mill. Let me tell you, that place and I go way back. When I was a lawyer, we ran more court cases to stop that proposed dirty, stinking pulp mill than to stop any other proposed development in this nation. We challenged every single state and federal government approval. This was because that site in the Tamar Valley is not the place for a pulp mill. The noise that the pulp mill would have generated and the light that the pulp mill would have emitted would have been grossly disruptive to the residents of the Tamar Valley, and it would have permanently damaged the then $50-million-a-year tourism industry. The massive amounts of water that the pulp mill would have needed could not have been delivered, because the presence of threatened flora species where the pipeline was intended to be built would have prohibited it. For all these reasons, the pulp mill failed.

For the same reasons, a noisy, light-emitting and water intensive AI data centre at the same site as the proposed Gunns pulp mill cannot proceed, in what is now a $100-million-a-year tourism industry. It might have local council approval, but I can't see how it could get federal government approval under our national environment laws. Big business and the Tasmanian government sought to ram through the pulp mill, but, as a community, we stood up and saw it off. As a community, we can and we will do the same for this AI data centre.

We know that data centres are deeply unpopular across the whole of Australia, particularly in Tasmania. A petition tabled this month by my Greens colleagues in Tasmania's state parliament opposing the development of AI data centres was one of the largest in the state's history. Tasmanians called for an immediate moratorium on non-complete artificial intelligence and data facilities until strict protective guardrails are put in place.

We need a moratorium on AI data centre developments across the whole nation now. That is the Greens position and that is the public's expectation of all of us in this place. We can't wait until next year, when this government says it's going to introduce proposed laws, because, in the meantime, companies like Firmus are going to ram their proposals through local planning processes. Local councils aren't even equipped to deal with that. AI data centres were not even a sparkle in anyone's eye when the planning schemes were prepared. The only people that benefit from these developments are the big tech corporations.

The company that is seeking to build the data centre in Tasmania's Tamar Valley, Firmus, is run by a convicted fraudster. Can we really take him at his word? We can't, and I'll give you some evidence as to why. Firmus has just appealed the local council decision to approve the data centre at the proposed Gunns pulp mill site in an effort to allow it to run diesel powered generators at the site. It had promised that its data centres would be powered by renewable energy.

These big tech corporations are misleading our communities. They are misleading our governments, and they are proposing developments that are in the wrong place. The community won the fight against Gunns proposed pulp mill and the community will win this fight against this proposed AI data centre.

speaker: Fatima Payman
heading: DOCUMENTS
subheading: Cybersafety Legislation; Order for the Production of Documents
text:
I move:

That the Senate take note of the explanation.

When you make a mistake, you should own up to it. In August, officials from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts told the Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee that certain broken links in the Ageassurance technology trial report were not broken at the time the report was handed over. This evidence, the department said, was based on evidence from the company behind the report, the UK-based Age Check Certification Scheme. It was later revealed that ACCS had lied to the Guardian Australia and Australian age-check provider KJR by claiming that AI had not been used in the preparation of the report when, in fact, it had. When asked whether the department had verified that the links had only become broken after the report was presented, an official grumbled, 'It's very difficult to go back and check what may have been replaced a year ago.'

Now, I'm not normally one to put on the tinfoil hijab, but there was something off about all this. So I took on this 'difficult task' and investigated the department's claim. Using a digital library of archived webpages, I was able to confirm that these links pointed to the wrong papers when they were supposedly accessed and when the report was handed to government. Dr Reuben Kirkham, a former computer science academic, told the committee that the existence of this archival evidence 'puts the position beyond any real doubt'.

I noted in a dissenting report that, on evidence I had seen, ACCS had misled the department and that, based on this misleading advice, the department had misled the committee. I do not believe that the department set out to mislead the committee, but I did describe the failure of the department to verify ACCS's claim as a serious dereliction of duty and recommended that the department review the incident to determine whether a breach of the APS Code of Conduct had occurred. Not only was I able to disprove the department's claim but I was able to do it so very easily. Aren't these guys supposed to be the experts? I understand that these are very serious allegations, and I do not make them lightly.

In response, the secretary of the department wrote to the chair of the committee about this issue. The secretary wrote:

I do not accept the conclusion that officials are failing in their duties if they give evidence to a committee based on advice provided to them that, at face value, can be accepted as accurate.

The representations made by officials were based on information available to them at the time and were honestly and reasonably held.

There was not one word contesting what I had said, but nor was there one word taking accountability for providing misleading evidence to a committee of the Senate. There was no acknowledgement that these officials had provided false evidence based on advice from ACCS, who have lied to multiple parties, including the government, about this report. It doesn't seem like ACCS will be penalised for this, which sends an unacceptable message: you can win contracts paid by the taxpayer, deliver shoddy work, lie to the government about it and get away with it. There won't even be a departmental investigation. It just isn't good enough. It's inevitable that the department's evidence will be revealed to be, without a doubt, incorrect. Despite this, the department has yet to acknowledge its misleading evidence, let alone apologise to the committee. Even the liars at ACCS have come out and apologised for what they now describe as 'outdated or incorrect links'. This saga of obfuscation will be for nothing.

When I brought to the attention of the Commonwealth Grants Commission that it appeared to have provided misleading evidence to the Economics Legislation Committee during estimates, it was quick to not only clarify what its evidence should have been but apologise for the error. This is the gold standard for APS accountability. Meanwhile, the department has provided incomplete responses to questions on notice and dragged out FOI timelines. It has failed to take accountability for the mistakes it has made. Years from now, these actions will make for an unseemly tale of resistance to scrutiny.

speaker: Ian Sollom
heading: Attorney General’s Office
text: Fraud is growing, and artificial intelligence is making it easier for it to be committed at scale. While cases can be complex, all too often victims tell me that they feel abandoned by the system. The CPS strategy folds fraud into organised crime and national security issues, and none of its seven priorities is actually about victims; in that regard, it differs from the previous economic crime strategy. How will the Solicitor General ensure that fraud victims are not lost in the CPS’s new approach?

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, I beg leave to ask the Question standing in my name on the Order Paper. In doing so, I draw attention to my AI and digital interests set out in the register.

speaker: Tim Watts
heading: GRIEVANCE DEBATE
subheading: Australian Defence Force Parliamentary Program, Artificial Intelligence
text:
'Everyday people doing extraordinary things'—that's the way Commander Paul Hardman described the work of his outstanding crew on HMAS Choules, who generously hosted me recently as part of the Australian Defence Force Parliamentary Program. I couldn't agree more with him, and I was proud as an Australian to have the opportunity to see it up close in person.

The ADF Parliamentary Program allows members of this place to step into the shoes of the Australian servicemen and servicewomen who we ask so much of as a nation. It gives MPs a meaningful insight into the day-to-day operations of the ADF through practical, immersive experiences. We get the opportunity to experience their workplaces, share their daily routines and gain a much deeper understanding of their lives and the responsibilities that they carry on behalf of Australia every day. I've participated in the program four times now, and I've always walked away with a feeling of deep pride in being able to see Australians in the ADF executing what they have been trained to do in the field.

I also want to put on the record that, in the decade that I've participated in the program, I've personally observed the way that the culture of the ADF, like this parliament, has changed. I was proud to see the diversity of modern Australia reflected in the young service men and women that I saw on this program. Real progress has been made on this front, and I want to recognise it here in this place.

This year in the ADFPP, I joined the ADF personnel taking part in exercise Keris Woomera 2026. Exercise Keris Woomera is a major bilateral military exercise conducted between the Australian Defence Force and the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and it was established by this government in 2024. The name Keris Woomera tells a story. The kris is a traditional Indonesian dagger, the woomera a traditional Australian spear thrower. Together they symbolise two distinct traditions working together towards a common purpose. That symbolism is important because this exercise is about far more than military exercises. It's about trust. It's about understanding. It's about building the habits of cooperation that allow two neighbouring countries to work effectively together when it matters most. Around 1,000 ADF personnel and over 1,200 TNI members participated in the exercise and conducted complex training across maritime, land, air and cyber domains. It's a significant exercise and a key element of our broader Indo-Pacific Endeavour program. The exercise is designed to strengthen interoperability, enhance combined operational capabilities and further deepen defence cooperation between Australia and Indonesia.

As part of KW 2026, I bunkered down with the REM on HMAS Choules, embarked on amphibious vehicles to land on the east coast of Java near Banyuwangi, slept in barracks with an artillery unit and experienced the South-East Asian heat in uniform with protective gear.

KW 2026 was a significant exercise for multiple reasons. It was the first time Australia's High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, HIMARS, was deployed and fired overseas. KW 2026 was also the first time that RAAF No. 4 Squadron deployed aircraft into South-East Asia since the Second World War. It was also the first time that Australia conducted cyberintegration training with Indonesia.

Participating in exercise Keris Woomera gave me the opportunity to observe something that's increasingly important in Australia's security and prosperity: the partnership between Australia and Indonesia. Australia and Indonesia are good neighbours and close partners. We're bound by strategic trust, mutual respect and a shared interest in a peaceful, stable and prosperous region. Earlier this year, Prime Minister Albanese and President Prabowo signed the Australia-Indonesia Treaty on Common Security, the Jakarta treaty. That treaty reflects a close friendship, partnership and deep trust between Australia and Indonesia. At its core is a simple idea: to keep Australia and Australians secure, we have to anchor our security in our region. Exercises like Keris Woomera show what that looks like in practice. They deepen understanding between our people and help build the habits of partnership that contribute to peace, stability and security across the region.

What struck me most during the exercise was not the equipment, impressive though it was, nor the complexity of the planning. It was the people. The Australian Defence Force and TNI are building something that no agreement or exercise directive can create on its own: trust—trust that comes from training together, solving problems together, spending time together. I had the opportunity to speak to both ADF members and TNI personnel throughout the exercise, and again and again I heard the same thing: they genuinely enjoy working together as partners. They value the opportunity to learn from one another. They appreciate the different perspectives each side brings. They recognise that every exercise strengthens relationships that may one day prove critical when our countries are called on to work together.

I acknowledge and thank all those who made my participation in exercise Keris Woomera possible. I want to thank my in-country liaison officer—makasih pak. I thank Lieutenant Alec Fuller for sharing an early-morning picket with me in Java. I thank Colonel Mark Tutton, Commander Landing Force of the Australian Amphibious Force; Captain Christopher Doherty, RAN, Commander Australian Amphibious Task Group; Commander Paul Hardman, the commanding officer of the HMAS Choules; Bombardier Max Vaughan, who demonstrated how to make things go bang on Java; and all of the ADF personnel who hosted us throughout the exercise, including my cabinmate on the Choules, Lieutenant Elliot Mitchell. Thank you also, as always, to Lieutenant Colonel Andy Martin, who does the important work of preparing all Australian parliamentarians to participate in the program. And I want to recognise Lieutenant Colonel Brett Edmonds, who I hosted in my office as part of the ADF parliamentary exchange before his departure. You're a credit to the ADF. Thank you also to all the Australian service men and women for our country.

Deputy Prime Minister Marles recently said that artificial intelligence is 'as big a sovereignty inflection point as we've seen since the Second World War'. He's right. A commitment from a frontier AI lab to train their models here could be the foundation of a new Australian-based AI industry that powers our security and prosperity in the decades to come. Hosting the training of frontier AI models in Australia could greatly expand the range of choices available to Australia in the rapidly changing and uncertain world we are seeing emerging around us. But the terms of that investment matter. Done right, it could commit the labs to invest in Australian researchers, put compute in the hands of Australian universities and start-ups and deal Australia into a seat at the table where the rules on the regulations and safety of frontier AI get written.

If Australia hosted an internationally significant share of the world's training compute, our voice would carry further with the labs and with other governments. We'd be wired into the supply chain of an industry that will shape the coming decades. We'd make ourselves indispensable. None of this will just happen, though. The labs have choices about where they invest. They weigh energy, talent, law and politics, and other countries are courting them. Winning this investment will take what Australia used to do best: an approach of our own—one that shapes things in the Australian way.

The Prime Minister has stated that the work with his framework on Australian standards for AI is intended to do this. The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence has backed it. A letter to the Prime Minister from the committee on 12 October, signed by the chair and the deputy chair, said that Australia should not merely be 'a consumer of AI technologies developed elsewhere, but a trusted, competitive and strategically capable partner of the global AI industry'. The letter asks that any deal with the labs reserve compute for national security and our universities. It asks that the Australian Signals Directorate be given early access to new models.

But the committee also heard that there's a real obstacle to being able to realise investment in frontier AI model training in Australia. In my first speech in this place, in 2013, I noted that Australian intellectual property law was throwing sand in the gears of digital innovation and limiting Australian productivity growth. American copyright law has built the most rewarding economy for content creators in world history. Home to the biggest film and music industries in the world, Hollywood and the Grammys, as well as a video game industry bigger than both of them put together, it's a great place to be a filmmaker, musician, writer or artist. But US copyright law also allows transformative uses of content—using existing work to create something completely different. This kind of transformative use is the foundation of digital innovation, and there may be no better example of this transformative use than generative AI.

Generative AI doesn't substitute or compete with the products that it learns from. It learns from them and creates something completely new. American courts have ruled on training for generative AI and so far have found it to be a fair use. Australian law has no similar legislative protection for transformative uses. As a result, the work of Australian artists, musicians and journalists is currently being used to train generative AI models in the United States—in the words of the committee's letter to the PM—'without adequate control or payment'. At the same time, it's also why no frontier AI labs are training models here.

The evidence before the committee is clear: the status quo doesn't work for anyone—not the creators, not the labs, not the Australian national interest—nor does it maximise our sovereignty. And that's what the committee's letter to the PM said. It asked the government to re-examine our copyright settings so that creators keep control and get paid to build a better outcome for Australia—one that, if we can reach it, will be a world-leading settlement. Last month, at the National Press Club, former prime minister Kevin Rudd warned that Australia could slide into becoming a second-rate country. Missing opportunities like this is what would make us one.

speaker: Alan Campbell
heading: Business of the House
text:
As ever, I thank the hon. Gentleman for the hard work he does as Chair of the Backbench Business Committee, and indeed the rest of the Committee for the work they do. I join him in paying tribute to Sir John Hannam, who was a distinguished Member of this House. We send our condolences to his friends and family.

I thank the hon. Gentleman for what he said about future Back-Bench business and about the AI debate. The hon. Member for Carshalton and Wallington (Bobby Dean) should not underestimate the influence that he has in this place, because he has got half an answer—if not the whole answer—on exactly when it will be. I will look at allocating time. As the hon. Member for Harrow East (Bob Blackman) knows, I will do my very best to do that.

I send my best wishes to the Hindu community for Diwali. As ever, the hon. Gentleman raises very important concerns about social cohesion and faith groups, not just in this country but abroad. I put on the record my thanks to the Hindu community for everything that they do in our local communities and across the country.

I will also raise the hon. Gentleman’s concerns with the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. He has raised these matters before. The Government take the treatment of minority communities, and particularly faith communities, very seriously indeed. I will raise it with FCDO colleagues and see whether, at some point, we can get the statement that he seeks.

speaker: Lord Leong
heading: Small and Medium-sized Enterprises: AI Sector - Question
text: My Lords, the Government’s core evidence is the AI sector study. The 2024 study found that SMEs make up 96% of UK AI firms, and nearly 90% of firms surveyed expected revenue growth within a year. To encourage investment, the sovereign AI fund, backed by up to £500 million, invests directly in British AI start-ups, alongside free compute through the AI research resource, Innovate UK’s £130 million growth catalyst, and a £100 million R&D procurement scheme.

speaker: Adam Dance
text:
Sorry—I totally agree with the hon. Member. It is really good to have cross-party support. Just as the Prime Minister has argued that we need mayors as a force to drive change in local authorities’ areas, we need one person in Government to drive positive change on neurodiversity policy.

You are probably thinking, “Adam, that is all great, but how are you actually going to do it?” To put it simply, I am asking the Government to do three things: first, to make way for a new Minister by restructuring current posts or amending the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975 to expand the number of Ministers we can have; secondly, to give the new Minister funded statutory powers, by presenting Parliament with a cross-departmental strategy for neurodiversity that the Minister would be responsible for implementing, because this does not work if the Minister does not have teeth; and thirdly, to appoint a Minister for neurodiversity, which is probably the most difficult and political part of the whole process.

That is obviously easier said than done, but, as with most things, the answer is there: it just requires political willpower. Look at the new Minister for Artificial Intelligence post in the Cabinet Office. We see this time and again with Government: we are told, “Oh, that is too complicated,” or, “Oh, that wouldn’t be practical,” but then the public kick up a fuss, and, suddenly, it is not too difficult and can actually be done rather quickly. Let us not forget that this is about 20% of the public.

Obviously, though, the Minister today cannot snap her fingers and promise to do this—I would love it if she could. That is just not how this works, and I get that. Instead, I ask the Minister to commit today to starting the process by having civil servants review cross-departmental policy on neurodiversity and the merits of a neurodiversity Minister, and then to meeting me and campaigners to talk through the findings with us and hear our suggestions in more detail.

I know that this proposal is ambitious, but it is the lack of ambition on neurodiversity policy that has got us into this mess in the first place. It is only with bold action that we are going to make a difference, because I do not want to live in a country where the next generation of neurodiverse kids feel as I did when they tried to shut my youth club, and where decision makers just do not get it and just do not care. I thank everybody for listening.
